fields.title: What p95 and p99 mean
fields.keyTakeaway: Percentiles show how many people have a bad experience, while averages hide it, and the tail multiplied by the number of requests per session stops being a rare edge case.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: What do three numbers in a report mean: p50 = 180 ms, p95 = 1.4 s, p99 = 6.2 s?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A target without a specified percentile is unachievable by definition: there will always be a request slower than any threshold. Such a target is either ignored or generates endless tail optimization.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: A [[percentile|percentile]] is the value below which a given share of measurements falls.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: p50 (median): half the requests are faster. p95: 95% are faster, 5% are slower. p99: 1% are slower.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: The three numbers from the question read as follows: a typical user waits 180 ms, every twentieth user waits more than one and a half seconds, and every hundredth waits more than six.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Why the [[mean|average]] lies.** Response time has an asymmetric distribution: the minimum is constrained by physics, while the maximum is unbounded. A few very slow requests skew the average without showing how many there are. An average of 200 ms is compatible with both a uniform distribution and a scenario where 95% take 50 ms and 5% take 3 seconds.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **How many people are behind the tail.** 1% at 6.3 million requests per day is 63 thousand requests. If one user makes 25 requests per session, the probability of encountering at least one slow request per session at p99 = 6 seconds is about 22%. That is, every fifth person sees a six-second delay at least once per visit.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: This arithmetic is the main takeaway: **the tail, multiplied by the number of requests per session, stops being a tail.** This is why targets are set using p95 and p99 rather than the average.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: What to look at alongside percentiles: a [[histogram|histogram]] shows the shape. Two humps usually mean two different paths—for example, a cache hit and a miss.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Checkout: p50 = 640 ms, p95 = 2.1 s, p99 = 11 s.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: The 11-second p99 turned out to be almost entirely due to the payment provider—the exact one whose p95 is 14 seconds according to the contract. Our tail was someone else's tail.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Per-user calculation: with 20 thousand checkouts per day, 1% is 200 people daily waiting more than 11 seconds on the payment screen. With a 19% churn at peak, these 200 people are a noticeable part of the problem.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: A separate discovery when analyzing the catalog histogram: two humps at 80 ms and 900 ms. The first is a cache hit, the second is a miss. The hit rate turned out to be 71%, not 95% as believed. The problem was not speed, but the fact that caching worked twice as poorly as expected.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: p99.9 and higher are noisy at low volumes: at a thousand requests, that is a single measurement. Looking at them makes sense only at scale.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Percentiles show how many people have a bad experience, while averages hide it, and the tail multiplied by the number of requests per session stops being a rare edge case.
